main.title: Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue!
main.subtitle: An ordinary house becomes a toy-sized adventure
main.summary: Traveller’s Tales built Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue! around the toys’ journey to save Woody from Al. Released in 1999, the three-dimensional platformer lets Buzz explore familiar places from a toy’s perspective: Andy’s house, the neighbourhood and a construction site become enormous obstacle courses. The original PlayStation game spans fifteen levels. Rather than simply replaying the film’s scenes, its spaces turn shelves, furniture and building equipment into surfaces to climb, jump across and investigate.

cards.heading: Buzz goes after Woody
cards.text: Traveller’s Tales built Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue! around the toys’ journey to save Woody from Al. Released in 1999, the three-dimensional platformer lets Buzz explore familiar places from a toy’s perspective: Andy’s house, the neighbourhood and a construction site become enormous obstacle courses. The original PlayStation game spans fifteen levels. Rather than simply replaying the film’s scenes, its spaces turn shelves, furniture and building equipment into surfaces to climb, jump across and investigate.

cards.heading: Five tasks, many routes
cards.text: Pizza Planet Tokens measure progress. Regular levels offer five tasks, including collecting coins for Hamm, defeating a miniboss, finding missing objects, solving a puzzle and completing a race or timed challenge. Advancing requires enough tokens overall, not every token in every level. Buzz combines a double jump with ledge climbing, laser shots and a spinning attack; his wings assist the jump rather than granting unrestricted flight. Helping Mr. Potato Head recover lost parts unlocks useful equipment. The original manual credits Andy Blythe and Marten Joustra of Swallow Studios for the game’s original music, distinguishing this score from the film soundtrack.

main.title: Crazy Taxi
main.summary: Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega.

cards.heading: Every fare is a race against time
cards.text: Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega. It is the first game in the Crazy Taxi series. In the game, players are tasked with picking up taxi customers and driving to their destination as quickly as possible. It was first released in arcades in 1999 then ported to other consoles starting with the Sega Dreamcast in 2000.

cards.heading: An arcade idea finds a home audience
cards.text: The game received generally positive reviews across most versions, with the Dreamcast port garnering critical acclaim. Critics praised its difficulty curve and the gameplay as "addictive". Reception to the implementation of the soundtrack was more mixed. In retrospect, Crazy Taxi has been regarded as one of the greatest video games of all time. It became one of the few Sega All Stars on the Dreamcast and earned Greatest Hits and Player's Choice status on PlayStation 2 and GameCube respectively. The game has been rereleased numerous times, and was featured on the Dreamcast Collection in 2011. The core gameplay of Crazy Taxi has inspired other games and numerous clones. The game's success on consoles prompted Sega to continue the series, starting with Crazy Taxi 2 in 2001.

main.title: Quake III Arena
main.summary: Quake III Arena is a 1999 first-person shooter game developed by id Software.

cards.heading: Multiplayer becomes the main event
cards.text: Quake III Arena is a 1999 first-person shooter game developed by id Software. The third installment of the Quake series, it focuses primarily on multiplayer gameplay, becoming one of the first modern arena shooters. While the single-player mode in previous installments were story-based, in Arena it is reduced to a player versus environment variant of the core multiplayer mode.

cards.heading: Movement and customisation
cards.text: Notable features of Quake III Arena include a minimalist design, very extensively customizable settings such as field of view, texture detail and enemy model; and advanced movement features such as strafe-jumping and rocket-jumping. It features music composed by Sonic Mayhem and Front Line Assembly founder Bill Leeb.

cards.heading: An arena for organised competition
cards.text: The game was praised by reviewers who, for the most part, described the gameplay as fun and engaging. Many liked the crisp graphics and focus on multiplayer. Quake III Arena, often being considered one of the greatest video games ever made, has also been used extensively in professional electronic sports tournaments such as QuakeCon, Cyberathlete Professional League, DreamHack, and the Electronic Sports World Cup.

main.title: Tekken Tag Tournament
main.summary: Tekken Tag Tournament is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: A two-on-two arcade Dream Match
cards.text: Tekken Tag Tournament is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It is a spin-off of the Tekken series. Not canon to the main storyline, Tekken Tag Tournament features nearly all the characters in the previous Tekken games and introduces a two-on-two 'tag team' battle mechanic. It was released as an arcade game, before becoming a North American and European launch title for the PlayStation 2 in 2000. The arcade version ran on the same Namco System 12 board with a 32-bit engine as Tekken 3, while the ported home console version received upgraded graphics.

cards.heading: A sequel and an HD return
cards.text: A follow-up, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, was released in 2011. A remastered version of the game titled Tekken Tag Tournament HD was released for the PlayStation 3 in November 2011, as part of Tekken Hybrid.

main.title: Super Smash Bros.
main.subtitle: Four Nintendo characters share an arena
main.summary: Nintendo released Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 64 in Japan on January 21, 1999.

cards.heading: A different kind of fighting game
cards.text: Nintendo released Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 64 in Japan on January 21, 1999. Mario, Link, Pikachu, Kirby and other characters fight across platform-filled arenas. Hits raise a damage percentage, making opponents easier to launch beyond the stage. Four-player matches, items and different character weights and attacks create a fighting game centred on position and recovery.

cards.heading: The Dragon King prototype
cards.text: Masahiro Sakurai's prototype was called Dragon King: The Fighting Game. He handled planning, specifications, graphics, modelling and movement, while Satoru Iwata programmed almost the entire project during weekends. Four anonymous figures tested battles designed around Nintendo 64's analogue stick. The Nintendo characters were introduced later, after the team had developed the basic rules.

cards.heading: Damage changes the danger of a hit
cards.text: Accumulated damage increases how far a fighter can be knocked by an attack. The edge of the stage becomes increasingly dangerous, and survival can require jumping or using an ability to return to a platform. An attack's value changes with the opponent's percentage and position. Players must decide when to pursue a finishing hit and when to concentrate on recovering safely.

cards.heading: Four players and changing items
cards.text: Nintendo 64's four controller ports support Sakurai's planned four-player battles without an adapter. A shared camera follows the fighters across arenas built around clear platforms. Items temporarily alter attacks and movement, while teams and handicaps let groups adjust the match. Distinct character silhouettes and directional attacks help players follow the action as all four compete.

main.title: Zombie Revenge
main.subtitle: The undead within arm’s reach
main.summary: Zombie Revenge is Sega's 1999 arcade brawler, followed by a Dreamcast version in Japan that November.

cards.heading: The undead within arm’s reach
cards.text: Zombie Revenge is Sega's 1999 arcade brawler, followed by a Dreamcast version in Japan that November. Three AMS agents enter a city overrun by the undead, using guns, hand-to-hand attacks and found weapons to fight towards the source of the outbreak. The action brings the monsters close enough to punch and throw, turning the player from an aiming observer into a character moving through the crowd. One or two players can take part, sharing the task of controlling the dangerous space around them.

cards.heading: Choose how to handle the next crowd
cards.text: Stick Breitling, Linda Rotta and Rikiya Busujima differ in their strengths and their proficiency with guns and close combat. Choosing a character changes how the next group is best approached, while weapons offer temporary alternatives. Boss encounters interrupt the advance through the city with larger threats. Switching between a firearm and a nearby opponent keeps distance relevant throughout the fighting: the safest target to shoot can cease to be the most urgent one when another zombie closes from the side.

cards.heading: Another route into the House of the Dead
cards.text: Developed by Sega AM1 and Data East, the game grew from the world of The House of the Dead and retains references to that series. Its arcade hardware was Sega's NAOMI, closely related to Dreamcast, which received the home conversion. That version also adds a one-on-one Battle Mode. Zombie Revenge carries the series' theatrical horror into another arcade tradition, using cooperative brawling and character movement to give familiar undead encounters a different pace and a more physical point of contact.

main.title: Armored Core: Master of Arena
main.subtitle: Climb the rankings to reach one pilot
main.summary: Armored Core: Master of Arena is FromSoftware's third PlayStation mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 4 February 1999. A survivor joins the Raven's Nest to confront Hustler One, the pilot blamed for the battle that killed their family. The journey gives the Arena a central place, turning a sequence of ranked opponents into the route towards a personal objective. Missions and machine customisation remain part of the campaign, but the next rival supplies a clear reason to return to the garage and improve the build.

cards.heading: Climb the rankings to reach one pilot
cards.text: Armored Core: Master of Arena is FromSoftware's third PlayStation mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 4 February 1999. A survivor joins the Raven's Nest to confront Hustler One, the pilot blamed for the battle that killed their family. The journey gives the Arena a central place, turning a sequence of ranked opponents into the route towards a personal objective. Missions and machine customisation remain part of the campaign, but the next rival supplies a clear reason to return to the garage and improve the build.

cards.heading: Prepare for the opponent, not only the mission
cards.text: The Arena concentrates combat on the capabilities of another Armored Core. Equipment, movement and weapon choice have to work against a rival who can exploit the player's weaknesses. Save data from either earlier PlayStation game can be imported, preserving a machine and parts already earned. That continuity gives experienced players a head start without removing the need to adapt. A new opponent can expose a familiar build's limitations, turning the ranking ladder into a series of practical questions about how the machine should be changed.

cards.heading: Make a rival of your own
cards.text: Ranker MK allows custom opponents to be created and then fought in the Arena, giving the workshop another purpose beyond the player's own machine. The feature extends the pleasure of assembly into the opposition itself: a design can become something to test against. Music by Kota Hoshino, Tsukasa Saitoh and Keiichiro Segawa accompanies the final release of the original PlayStation trilogy. North America received the game in 2000, while Europe missed an original release. Armored Core 2 then carried the series' garage and mercenary career onto PlayStation 2.

main.title: Final Fantasy VIII
main.subtitle: Junction, Memory and Adolescence
main.summary: Final Fantasy VIII begins with young people training for a profession that sends them into a war.

cards.heading: Students on the front line
cards.text: Final Fantasy VIII begins with young people training for a profession that sends them into a war. Squall belongs to Balamb Garden, a school for mercenaries, and becomes a member of SeeD. Released for PlayStation in Japan in 1999, the game moves between school life, military assignments and his growing relationship with Rinoa.

cards.heading: Magic becomes equipment
cards.text: Guardian Forces do more than appear as summoned creatures. Junctioning them opens abilities and lets stored magic improve a character's statistics. Draw supplies spells from enemies and other sources. Because a spell can be both something to cast and something to keep equipped, the inventory becomes part of character building.

cards.heading: A second life in cards
cards.text: Triple Triad places a compact card game inside this much larger journey. Its cards can be collected and played against people encountered along the way. Alongside the main battles and scenes, it gives towns and schools another reason to be revisited: someone there may have a hand worth challenging.

main.title: Power Stone
main.subtitle: The whole room is in the fight
main.summary: Capcom’s arena fighter turns furniture, space and three transforming gems into the tools of a two-player duel.

cards.heading: A fight across the room
cards.text: Power Stone is Capcom’s three-dimensional arena fighting game, first released in Japanese arcades on 13 February 1999 and brought to Dreamcast later that month. Its adventurers search for legendary stones said to grant a wish, meeting in colourful rooms and outdoor arenas along the way. Each duel allows the fighters to run around the space, jump towards an opponent and turn objects into weapons. A table or chair becomes part of the encounter, giving the room a more active role than a decorative backdrop.

cards.heading: Three stones change the balance
cards.text: Three Power Stones allow a fighter to transform into a much stronger version of themselves. Gathering them changes the immediate purpose of movement: reaching a loose stone can become more urgent than landing another ordinary hit. The transformed character gains powerful attacks, but the advantage lasts only while a separate meter remains. Spending it on a special move creates a short burst of power. The opponent must then decide whether to contest the stones, keep away for a moment or risk closing the distance.

cards.heading: A Dreamcast gathering
cards.text: The Dreamcast adaptation brought this compact arcade duel into a home setting suited to repeated matches. Players could learn an arena’s furniture and routes, then watch a familiar room produce a different exchange when someone reached a stone first. Tetsuya Shibata’s soundtrack accompanies a cast with exaggerated transformations and contrasting fighting styles. The first game concentrates on two opponents, leaving the space readable enough to follow their pursuit around the room. Power Stone 2 would build on that foundation with four-player battles and changing stages.

main.title: Silent Hill
main.summary: Silent Hill is a 1999 survival horror video game developed by Konami's Team Silent and published by Konami for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Harry searches for his daughter
cards.text: Silent Hill is a 1999 survival horror video game developed by Konami's Team Silent and published by Konami for the PlayStation. It is the first installment in the Silent Hill video game series. The game follows Harry Mason as he searches for his missing adopted daughter in the eponymous fictional American town of Silent Hill. Stumbling upon a cult conducting a rite to revive a deity it worships, he discovers her true origin. Five game endings are possible, depending on the actions taken by the player, including one joke ending.

cards.heading: Fog, darkness and a real-time town
cards.text: Unlike earlier survival horror games that used pre-rendering backgrounds, Silent Hill uses a third-person view with real-time rendering of 3D environments. To mitigate the limitations of the console hardware, developers used distance fog and darkness to obscure the graphics and omit pop-ins, which, in turn, helped establish the game's atmosphere and mystery. The player character of Silent Hill is an "everyman", unlike survival horror games focused on protagonists with combat training.

cards.heading: Psychological horror and its successors
cards.text: Silent Hill received positive reviews from critics upon its release and was commercially successful. It is considered by many to be one of the greatest video games ever made, as well as a defining title in the survival horror genre, moving away from the elements of the B movie horror genre to more psychological horror, emphasizing atmosphere. Various adaptations and expansions of Silent Hill have been released, including a 2001 visual novel, the 2006 feature film Silent Hill, and a 2009 reimagining of the game titled Silent Hill: Shattered Memories. The game was followed by Silent Hill 2 in 2001; a direct sequel, Silent Hill 3, in 2003; and a prequel, Silent Hill: Origins, in 2007. A remake by Bloober Team is in development.
